advances: Three prescribed facet traces at the centroid of a planar triangle, with arbitrary positive planar endpoints. No universal all-normal estimate is asserted at the middle centroid.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Let $D\subset K$ be the points in at least two centroid facet caps and write $J(Q)=|Q|-3|Q\cap D|$. We first prove $J(Q)\le2|K|/9$ for every compact convex $Q\subset K$, including those of zero area. Normalize by an affine change to $K=\{x,y\ge0:x+y\le3\}$ with centroid $g=(1,1)$ and area $9/2$. The regions covered by exactly one cap are three parallelograms, and those covered by exactly two are three triangles, up to boundaries of area zero. The integrand defining $J$ is respectively $1$ and $-2$.

Suppose $g$ is outside $\operatorname{int}Q$. A supporting or separating functional through $g$ is nonnegative on $Q$. Write it as $\sum_i a_i(\lambda_i-1/3)$ and choose $i$ minimizing $a_i$. On the interior of the cell exclusively covered by cap $i$, this equals $\sum_{j\ne i}(a_j-a_i)(\lambda_j-1/3)<0$, because the coefficients are not all equal. So $Q$ misses that open cell. Cutting by the trapezoid spanned by the other two exclusive cells removes only negative area, and cannot decrease $J$. To verify the geometry, permute barycentric coordinates so the excluded cell is the one where $\lambda_i=y/3>1/3$; the two remaining cells span $0\le y\le1,\ 0\le x\le3-y$. Its negative region is $1\le x\le2-y$, up to null boundaries.

For any convex subset of that trapezoid let $w(y)$ be its horizontal section length on its projection interval $I=[a_0,b_0]\subseteq[0,1]$. It is concave, nonnegative, and bounded by $3-y$. If the projection has length zero the area is zero. Otherwise $w$ is continuous in the interior and upper semicontinuous on $I$ by compactness. One-sided limiting values may be used at the endpoints without affecting area. An interval of length $w$ in $[0,3-y]$ has intersection with $[1,2-y]$ of length at least $\min(1-y,(w-1)_+)$. Indeed, if it meets both outside intervals it contains the middle one; otherwise at most one unit of its length lies outside the middle. The interval $[0,w]$ attains the bound. With $w=0$ off $I$ for integration, put $u=w-1$ and $V=\int_0^1(-u)_+$. The resulting upper bound for $J$ is $1-V+F$, where
$$
F=\int_0^1[-2u_++3(u+y-1)_+]\,dy.
$$
We show $F\le V$. The set where $u+y-1>0$ is an interval in $I$; if it has zero length then $F\le0$. Otherwise write its endpoints $t<r$. When $t=a_0$, the integrand is at most $2y-1$ on $(t,r)$ by $u\le2-y$, and nonpositive elsewhere. Thus $F\le\max(0,\int_{a_0}^1(2y-1)\,dy)=a_0(1-a_0)\le V$, since $w=0$ before $a_0$.

When $t>a_0$, let $c$ be the left endpoint in $I$ of $u\ge0$. Then $a_0\le c<t$, $u(c)\ge0$, $u(t)=1-t>0$, and $u(c)=0$ when $c>a_0$. Set $B_0=1-c$, $L=t-c$, $m=(1-t)/L$, so $L=B_0/(m+1)$ and $m>0$. Concavity gives $u(y)\ge m(y-c)$ on $[c,t]$ and $u(y)\le m(y-c)$ on $[t,r]$. Therefore
$$
F\le\max(0,F_*),\qquad
F_*=-mL^2+\int_t^1[\min(m(y-c),2-y)-3+3y]\,dy .
$$
The extension of the integral to $1$ in this maximum is valid because the displayed integrand is increasing, so the integral from $t$ to a variable right endpoint is convex. The two affine branches meet at $c+L+L/B_0$, which lies at or below $1$ exactly for $mB_0\ge1$. Integrating the two affine pieces gives
$$
F_*=\begin{cases}
(2cB_0m-1)/(2(m+1)),&mB_0\ge1,\\
B_0^2m(m-2)/(2(m+1)),&mB_0\le1.
\end{cases}
$$
For the deficit, $V\ge V_0=\int_0^c\min(1,m(c-y))\,dy$: when $c=a_0$ this follows from $w=0$ before $c$; when $c>a_0$, the chord from $c$ to $t$ bounds $u(y)\le m(y-c)$ on the projection before $c$. The integral $V_0$ is $mc^2/2$ for $mc\le1$ and $c-1/(2m)$ otherwise. In the first branch for $F_*$, $2(m+1)(V_0-F_*)=(mc-1)^2+3mc^2\ge0$ if $mc\le1$, and $2m(m+1)(V_0-F_*)=2(mc)^2+2mc-1>0$ if $mc>1$. In the second branch $F_*\le0$ for $m\le2$. For $m>2$, $mB_0\le1$ gives $mc\ge m-1>1$, hence $V_0>1/(2m)$ while $F_*\le(m-2)/(2m(m+1))<1/(2m)$. This proves $J(Q)\le1$ when $g$ is outside the interior.

If $g\in\operatorname{int}Q$, choose its shortest ray fraction $c>0$ from $g$ towards the three vertices of $K$. Permute barycentric coordinates so this is the ray $(1,1)$ in coordinates $(u,v)=(1-x,1-y)$ around $g$. The other rays are $(-2,1)$ and $(1,-2)$. Convexity puts $q=(c,c),(-2c,c),(c,-2c)$ in $Q$. A support line at $q$ has equation $\alpha u+\beta v=c(\alpha+\beta)$ with $Q$ on the lower side. Substitution of the other two points shows $\alpha,\beta\ge0$, and at least one is positive, so $Q$ has no point with $u>c,v>c$. The triangle of the three points contains $[0,c]^2$ and two adjacent double-covered triangles of total area $c^2$ with $uv\le0$, $u+v\ge0$. The positive-quadrant portion of $Q$ consists of the square and two wings, whose areas are $W_h,W_v$. In the horizontal wing put $M=\max (u-c)/(v+2c)$ over its closed range $u\ge c$, $0\le v\le c$. Its sections have width at most $M(v+2c)$, hence $W_h\le(5/2)Mc^2$. Join a maximizing point to $(c,-2c)$ and use convexity and the vertical segment at $u=c$. On $-c\le v\le0$, $Q$ contains the strip from $u=c$ to $u=c+M(v+2c)$. It lies in the adjacent double cone and contributes $(3/2)Mc^2\ge(3/5)W_h$ outside the two triangles. The swapped construction contributes at least $(3/5)W_v$ in the other cone; all overlaps of these contributions have area zero. The signed area in the cap $u+v\ge0$ is therefore at most $-c^2-(W_h+W_v)/5<0$. Its opposite half of $Q$ has $g$ on the boundary and signed area at most $1$ by the preceding argument. Add the two across their area-zero line. This proves the required signed-area estimate, with the original factor $2|K|/9$ restored.

Now for each $y\in B$ the translate-dilate $Q_y=(A+y)/2\subseteq K$ has area $a/4$. The estimate gives $4|Q_y\cap D|\ge a/3-8k/27=b/3+k/27=:c_*$. Apply a980c0ee5964ce1a to the closed relation $(x+y)/2\in D$ on $A\times B$. Its sections in $A$ have area at least $c_*>0$ and $a\ge b$, so a matching of mass at least $\min(b,c_*)$ extends to a coupling $\Pi$ with second marginal $1_B\,dy$ and first marginal at most $1_A\,dx$. Every midpoint is in at least one centroid facet cap because its barycentric coordinates sum to one; the matching outputs are in at least two. The sum of the three midpoint cap masses under $\Pi$ is therefore at least $b+\min(b,c_*)$. In each ambient halfspace the affine margin at the midpoint is the average of the endpoint margins, so the closed midpoint indicator is at most the sum of its two actual endpoint indicators. The two marginal bounds transfer the preceding lower bound to the total endpoint contribution across all three halfspaces. Each middle cap has area $4k/9$ by simplex dilation, giving $4k/3+b+\min(b,c_*)=4a/3+\min(2b/3,k/27)$. Divide by three for the single-cap consequence. If $b=0$, $a=k$ and each middle trace already contributes $4a/9$.
statement:
Let $A,K,B\subset\mathbb R^2$ be compact convex bodies of areas $a,k,b>0$ with $(A+B)/2\subseteq K$, $a=k+b$, and $K$ a triangle. Place them at bases $-1,0,1$, respectively, and let $\mu$ sum their actual planar areas. For every three closed ambient halfspaces $H_i$ whose middle traces on $K$ are its centroid facet caps $\{\lambda_i\ge1/3\}$, one has
$$
\sum_i\mu(H_i)\ge 4a/3+\min(2b/3,k/27)>4a/3.
$$
Thus one cap has mass at least $4a/9+\min(2b/9,k/81)$, exceeding $(4/9)\mu(\mathbb R^3)/2$ in the three-fiber model. If the right fiber has zero area and $a=k$, the three caps cannot all have mass below $4a/9$.
title: Three prescribed centroid facet caps with arbitrary planar endpoint shapes
